The nehu (Encrasicholina purpurea) is a small, short-lived engraulid endemic to the Hawaiian archipelago, where it plays a pivotal role as a forage fish supporting pelagic predators and local fisheries. Adults of this species attain a maximum recorded total body length of 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], a modest ultimate size that reflects its position near the lower end of the size spectrum within the family Engraulidae. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C], the embryonic development of this species is notably rapid, with the transition from fertilized egg to free-swimming prolarva occurring after approximately three days [ab = approximately three days]. This accelerated developmental tempo is consistent with the small egg size and high ambient temperature typical of subtropical pelagic spawners. The relatively brief incubation period likely confers advantages in terms of reducing the window of vulnerability for the demersal egg stage to benthic predation and physical disturbance in the nearshore waters where spawning aggregates are commonly observed.

Growth in nehu proceeds through a predictable sequence of larval and juvenile stages before the attainment of reproductive competence. Field-collected specimens indicate that the total length at which individuals first exhibit signs of gonadal development and reach puberty is approximately 4.0 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.0 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 0.42 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.42 grams], based on length-weight regressions derived from local populations. This length at maturity represents just over half of the species' ultimate length, a proportion that reflects an early-maturing life-history strategy typical of short-lived, high-mortality pelagic teleosts. Juveniles recruit to the adult population after undergoing metamorphosis, during which the body plan reorganizes from the slender, transparent larval form to the more robust, silver-flanked adult morphology. The rapid growth phase through the juvenile stage is energetically demanding, requiring sustained high feeding rates on zooplankton, particularly copepod nauplii and other microcrustaceans.

Reproductive output in nehu is characterized by extremely high fecundity and continuous spawning activity during the warmer months. Under the thermal conditions typical of Hawaiian nearshore waters (25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C]), mature females produce small, pelagic eggs that are broadcast-spawned into the water column. The daily reproductive rate, expressed as the number of eggs produced per female per year, is approximately 825 eggs annually [Ri = approximately 825 eggs annually], a value estimated from comparative data on the congener Stolephorus carpentariae and adjusted for the thermal regime. This translates into roughly 2.3 eggs per day when averaged over the reproductive season, a remarkably high sustained output for a fish of this body size. The individual eggs are minute, measuring approximately 0.8 millimeters in diameter, and upon fertilization and subsequent eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva possesses a wet weight at birth of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], derived from the spherical volume of the egg. This extraordinarily low neonatal mass underscores the extreme altricial state of the hatchling, which depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatching.

Longevity in nehu is constrained by a fast-paced life history, with the species exhibiting a maximum lifespan of approximately 183 days [am = approximately 183 days] under the thermal conditions of 25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C]. This abbreviated lifespan, representing roughly six months, is characteristic of short-lived tropical clupeiforms that rely on high early mortality and rapid turnover to sustain population abundance. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults, calculated from the length-weight relationship for Hawaiian nehu populations, reaches approximately 6.17 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.17 grams] for the largest individuals. This adult mass is modest even by engraulid standards, yet it supports a high metabolic demand driven by the warm-water environment and the energetic costs of continuous spawning. The relationship between body size and lifespan in this species follows the general pattern observed in small pelagics, where small body size and high metabolic rate are coupled with short generation times and rapid population cycles.

Comparative life-history analysis reveals that nehu occupies an extreme position along several axes of the fast-slow continuum among tropical marine fishes. The combination of a three-day incubation period (3 days) [ab = 3 days], a total length at puberty of 4.0 centimeters [Lp = 4.0 centimeters], and a maximum adult mass of 6.17 grams [Wwi = 6.17 grams] places it among the most rapidly maturing and shortest-lived of the commercially exploited engraulids at a temperature of 25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C]. By contrast, larger-bodied congeners in temperate waters often exhibit incubation periods exceeding one week and lifespans of several years. The nehu's brief maximal lifespan of roughly half a year (approximately 183 days) [am = approximately 183 days] necessitates an extraordinarily high reproductive investment, with females diverting a substantial proportion of somatic energy reserves into egg production at a temperature of 25.3 °C [T = 25.3 °C]. The wet weight at puberty, noted at 0.42 grams [Wwp = 0.42 grams], represents only about seven percent of the ultimate wet weight, indicating that reproductive maturation begins very early in the growth trajectory. This pattern is consistent with a life history optimized for high population turnover in an environment where predation pressure on adults is intense but food resources for larvae are seasonally abundant. Future work exploring the thermal sensitivity of these life-history traits under projected climate scenarios would be valuable for predicting population resilience.
